text: More than 200 years ago, Britain's wars with Napoleon brought hard times, and many people had no work.
The Luddites were English textile workers, who made cloth, and many of them were skilled at working machines.
src: The British economy suffered greatly from 1810 to 1812, with high unemployment and inflation, caused by the cost of the wars with Napoleon
The Luddites were English textile workers / many were skilled operators in the textile industry / the shearing frames and gig mills used to finish woollen cloth

text: Their movement began at Arnold, near Nottingham, and spread quickly through England.
They were not against all machines, only the ones that hurt their pay or made poor goods.
src: beginning at Arnold near Nottingham / spreads rapidly through England
They were not opposed to machines as such / concerns over workers’ pay, labour savings, child labour, working conditions and the quality of output

text: In Yorkshire, cloth workers called croppers broke the new machines with a hammer they named "Enoch".
They signed their letters with the name "Ned Ludd", a weaver from old stories.
src: In Yorkshire the croppers, who faced mass unemployment when Enoch Taylor of Marsden introduced cropping machines, broke the machines with a hammer they called “Enoch” to mock him
“Ned Ludd”, the legendary weaver or apprentice whose name signed their letters

text: Lord Byron was one of the few important people who spoke up for them.
src: Lord Byron was one of the few prominent defenders of the Luddites

text: The government sent 12,000 soldiers, and Parliament made breaking machines a crime punished by death.
After a big trial at York, some men were put to death or sent far away, and the movement ended.
src: Some 12,000 government troops / Parliament made machine-breaking a capital crime
the government staged a mass trial at York in January 1813 / the harsh sentences of those found guilty, which included execution and penal transportation, quickly ended the movement

text: They are still remembered in old songs, such as the Yorkshire folk song "The Cropper Lads".
Today, people who oppose new technology are sometimes called Luddites.
src: remembered in the Yorkshire folk song “The Cropper Lads” / the traditional song “The Triumph of General Ludd”
Today “Luddite” is sometimes used for anyone who opposes or resists new technologies
